disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by marked, persistent fear or anxiety about a clearly defined object or situation that is out of proportion to actual danger and leads to avoidance or significant distress and impairment. The fear response is typically immediate and consistent when the person encounters, or anticipates encountering, the phobic trigger, and the person often recognizes that the fear is excessive or unreasonable. Onset can occur in childhood or adulthood and the course is often chronic if untreated, though individuals may function well in other areas of life except where the phobic cue is involved. It is distinguished from social anxiety disorder and agoraphobia by the narrow, circumscribed nature of the feared stimulus and from PTSD or OCD by the absence of broader trauma-related syndromes or intrusive obsessions/compulsions driving the avoidance.

narrative.personality: Joby is a laid-back but meticulous hands-on craftsman who enjoys mentoring others, spending time outdoors, and improvising solutions on the job and in his hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Joby was installing custom cabinets on a second-floor renovation when a temporary railing failed and a coworker slipped, nearly pulling Joby over the edge before another crew member grabbed him; the coworker suffered a serious injury and Joby was left shaken by how close he’d come to falling. In the weeks that followed, he tried to push through and keep working on similar jobs, but he found himself increasingly tense whenever he had to work near exposed edges or climb certain types of ladders, quietly trading tasks with apprentices or reassigning himself to ground-level work. Over the next 11 months, this pattern hardened into a consistent avoidance of particular job sites and tasks, forcing him to turn down higher-paying framing and roofing work and rely more on shop-based projects, which strained his income and his sense of competence as a full-service carpenter. He finally sought psychiatric help after his boss warned him that his refusal to take on certain standard site assignments was jeopardizing both current contracts and his role as a mentor to apprentices.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Whenever I have to get back into that kind of spot at work, it hits me right away and I just freak out inside.”

narrative.personality: Tony is a disciplined, reflective pastor who combines methodical planning and financial stewardship with a deep reverence for tradition and commitment to community service.
narrative.stressor: Last year, Tony was invited to give an opening prayer and brief address at a large regional interfaith conference held in a historic cathedral, where elaborate staging and lighting were used to broadcast the event online; during a rehearsal, a stage-light rig malfunctioned and crashed to the floor just a few feet from him, showering the pulpit area with debris and forcing an abrupt evacuation. Though physically unharmed, he was deeply unsettled by the suddenness of the incident and the vulnerability he felt standing in an elevated, enclosed chancel with heavy equipment overhead, an image that lingered with him afterward. Over the ensuing months, he became increasingly reluctant to officiate services or ceremonies in similarly grand or structurally complex sanctuaries—especially when they involved overhead fixtures or elevated pulpits—going so far as to reroute weddings and joint services to simpler spaces and delegating certain liturgical duties to associates. As this avoidance began to interfere with key responsibilities, strained relationships with partner congregations, and conflicted with his own sense of vocation and leadership, he decided to seek psychiatric evaluation to understand why he now dreads stepping into certain worship spaces he once cherished.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve started going out of my way to avoid certain kinds of sanctuaries or setups because just being in them feels overwhelming.”

narrative.personality: Gary is a competitive, outgoing truck driver who thrives on being the center of attention, juggling work, community activities, and hands-on projects while still worrying about performance and deadlines.
narrative.stressor: Approximately 11 months ago, Gary was driving a long-haul route when a sudden mechanical failure caused his rig to fishtail on a wet highway; he narrowly avoided a multi-vehicle collision by steering onto the shoulder, where his truck partially jackknifed and left him shaken but physically uninjured. The scare rattled his usual confidence behind the wheel, and although he went back to driving soon after, he found himself increasingly distressed when he had to operate similar trucks on highways or in bad weather, volunteering for shorter local routes or sales calls he could make in smaller vehicles. Over time, this pattern of steering away from certain routes and vehicle types began to limit his availability for lucrative long-distance runs and created tension with his employer, who relied on his previously top-tier on-time performance. When his supervisor hinted that his route refusals might affect his position and he noticed himself dreading dispatch calls that might involve particular driving conditions, he agreed—after encouragement from his wife and coaching colleagues—to see a psychiatrist about what had changed in his relationship to the road.
narrative.chief_complaint: “If I know I’ve got to drive in that kind of situation again, I either find a way around it or white-knuckle it the whole time.”
